Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Cambodia and Thailand have agreed to redeploy some troops away from the site of a border temple at the center of a tense military standoff in its second week. Thai soldiers take a rest near the Preah Vihear temple in Preah Vihear province. The decision came after the two sides met to resolve the impasse. Government officials from both nations plan to meet again to decide how many troops will remain at the site of the Preah Vihear temple, the Thai News Agency reported Monday. At a later meeting, the two sides plan to discuss how to tackle the thorny issue at the center of the ongoing dispute -- the question of whether land around the temple belongs to Thailand or Cambodia. The 11th century temple sits atop a cliff on Cambodian soil but has its most accessible entrance on the Thai side. The two countries differ on whether some territory around the temple forms part of Thailand or Cambodia. The decision to redeploy troops took place after a Monday meeting in Siem Reap, Cambodia. Last week, an eight-hour meeting between Thai and Cambodian officials ended with both sides agreeing on only one point: that troops each country has amassed at the site of the temple will not fire on each other. The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962. Thailand claims, however, that the 1.8 square mile (4.6 sq. km) area around it was never fully demarcated. Thailand says the dispute arose from the fact that the Cambodian government used a map drawn during the French occupation of Cambodia -- a map that places the temple and surrounding area in Cambodian territory. This month, the United Nations approved Cambodia's application to have the temple listed as a World Heritage Site -- a place the U.N. says has outstanding universal value. The decision re-ignited tensions, with some in Thailand fearing it will make it difficult for their country to lay claim to disputed land around the temple. Opposition parties in Thailand used the issue to attack the government, which initially backed the heritage listing. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has been in power since 1985, portrayed the U.N. recognition as a national triumph in the run-up to the general elections. Analysts believe that the nationalist sentiments stirred up by the military standoff helped Hun Sen's ruling party win enough seats in Sunday's parliamentary elections so that it can form a government without the need for a coalition. The current flare-up began July 15, when Cambodian guards briefly detained three Thais who crossed into the area. Once they were let go, the three refused to leave the territory. Cambodia claims Thailand sent troops to retrieve the trio and gradually built up their numbers. Thailand denies that, saying its troops are deployed in Thai territory.

The redeployment agreement followed talks aimed at breaking the deadlock. According to the Thai News Agency on Monday, officials from both governments will hold another meeting to determine how many soldiers from each country will continue to be stationed near the temple.

A subsequent round of negotiations is expected to address the more difficult underlying question: whether the disputed land surrounding Preah Vihear belongs to Cambodia or Thailand.

The 11th-century temple stands on a cliff within Cambodian territory, although its easiest point of access is from Thailand. While the temple itself is in Cambodia, the two countries disagree over sovereignty of some nearby areas.

The troop-redeployment decision was reached during a meeting Monday in Siem Reap, Cambodia. At an eight-hour session the previous week, Cambodian and Thai representatives had managed to agree on only one matter—that the forces assembled by both countries near the temple would not shoot at one another.

In 1962, the International Court of Justice ruled that Preah Vihear belonged to Cambodia. Thailand nevertheless maintains that the surrounding 1.8-square-mile, or 4.6-square-kilometer, area was never completely demarcated.

Thai authorities say the disagreement stems from Cambodia’s reliance on a map produced during the French occupation. That map identifies both the temple and the land around it as Cambodian territory.

Earlier this month, the United Nations accepted Cambodia’s request to designate the temple as a World Heritage Site, a status reserved for locations the U.N. considers to possess outstanding universal value. The listing revived tensions because some Thais fear it could weaken Thailand’s ability to claim the contested territory around the site.

Thailand’s opposition parties used the controversy to criticize the government, which had originally supported the heritage designation. In Cambodia, Prime Minister Hun Sen—who has governed since 1985—presented the U.N. decision as a national victory ahead of the country’s general election.

Analysts say the nationalist feeling generated by the military confrontation helped Hun Sen’s ruling party secure enough seats in Sunday’s parliamentary election to establish a government without forming a coalition.

The latest dispute began on July 15, when Cambodian guards briefly held three Thai citizens who had entered the area. After being released, the three declined to leave. Cambodia alleges that Thailand dispatched troops to recover them and then steadily increased its military presence. Thailand rejects that account and insists its soldiers are positioned on Thai soil.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the latest developments in the 2008 Cambodia–Thailand border dispute, including the troop negotiations, competing territorial claims, and the history of Preah Vihear temple.
counterfactuals.output:
### 2008 troop standoff and negotiations

The immediate crisis began after UNESCO listed **Preah Vihear temple as a Cambodian World Heritage site on July 7, 2008**. Thai opponents argued that Bangkok’s support for the listing could weaken Thailand’s claim to nearby land. Political protests followed, and in mid-July Cambodian forces detained several Thai activists who had crossed the border near the temple. Both countries then deployed hundreds of troops, artillery, and other weapons to the area.

Initial military talks failed to produce an immediate withdrawal because each side insisted its troops were operating on its own territory. Later negotiations produced phased redeployments and temporary reductions, but they did not resolve the underlying border question. Tensions repeatedly returned, culminating in armed clashes in October 2008 that killed soldiers on both sides. Further fighting occurred intermittently through 2011.

### Competing territorial claims

Cambodia’s sovereignty over **the temple itself** was already established, but the two countries disagreed over surrounding territory—often described as roughly **4.6 square kilometres**—and over how the frontier should be mapped.

- **Cambodia** relied heavily on a French-era map that placed the temple and nearby ground on the Cambodian side.
- **Thailand** argued that the boundary should follow the natural watershed of the Dângrêk Mountains under the original Franco-Siamese treaties, which would place portions of the adjoining land in Thailand.
- Thailand said UNESCO’s listing should not determine the unresolved border; Cambodia maintained that Thai deployments violated its territory.

The dispute was therefore less about ownership of the temple than about the extent of Cambodian territory around it and access to the site.

### History of Preah Vihear

Preah Vihear is a Khmer Hindu temple complex, principally built between the **9th and 12th centuries** and dedicated to Shiva. It sits atop a cliff in the Dângrêk range. Although geographically easier to approach from Thailand, it is a major monument of the Khmer Empire and a powerful Cambodian national symbol.

The border ambiguity arose from early-20th-century treaties between Siam and French Indochina and from maps prepared during the subsequent survey. Thailand occupied the temple after French forces withdrew from Cambodia in 1954. Cambodia brought the case to the **International Court of Justice**, which ruled in **1962** that the temple belonged to Cambodia and ordered Thailand to withdraw its forces.

The judgment did not fully settle the surrounding boundary. In **2013**, after renewed fighting, the ICJ clarified that Cambodia held sovereignty over the temple’s entire promontory and that Thai personnel had to withdraw from that area, while leaving some broader boundary demarcation to bilateral negotiations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article explaining why Thai and Cambodian troops amassed near Preah Vihear, what their governments agreed to at the Siem Reap meeting, and how UNESCO’s World Heritage listing intensified tensions.
counterfactuals.output:
# Preah Vihear Listing Turned an Old Border Dispute Into a Military Standoff

**SIEM REAP, Cambodia —** The deployment of Thai and Cambodian troops around the ancient temple of Preah Vihear grew out of a combustible mix of an unfinished colonial-era border, domestic political turmoil in Thailand and Cambodia’s successful campaign to have the monument inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.

At talks in the Cambodian city of Siem Reap, the two governments agreed in principle to reduce and redeploy forces from the contested area and to continue negotiations through existing bilateral border mechanisms. The meeting lowered the immediate risk of an armed clash but did not resolve the central dispute: where the border runs across land adjoining the temple.

## Why troops gathered near the temple

Preah Vihear, an 11th-century Hindu sanctuary built along a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains, belongs to Cambodia. The International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that the temple was “situated in territory under the sovereignty of Cambodia” and ordered Thailand to remove troops and other personnel stationed there.

The judgment, however, did not fully demarcate the surrounding frontier. Thailand and Cambodia continued to disagree over nearby land, commonly described as a roughly 4.6-square-kilometer area. Cambodia relied heavily on a French-produced map drawn when it was under colonial rule, while Thailand argued that portions of the boundary should follow the watershed line specified in earlier Franco-Siamese agreements.

Geography added to the problem. Although the temple stands on the Cambodian side of the cliff, it was long more easily approached from Thailand. That practical access, combined with competing maps and an incompletely marked border, allowed disputes over adjacent ground to persist for decades.

The immediate crisis began in July 2008, shortly after UNESCO approved Cambodia’s application to list Preah Vihear as a World Heritage site. Three Thai activists crossed into the area to protest the listing and were detained by Cambodian authorities. Although they were soon released, Thai soldiers then moved into the vicinity.

Cambodia said the Thai troops had entered Cambodian territory, particularly around the Keo Sikha Kiri Svara Buddhist pagoda near the temple. Thailand maintained that its soldiers were operating in an undemarcated or disputed zone. Cambodia deployed additional forces in response, and within days hundreds of armed personnel from both countries were facing one another at close range.

Each government said its deployment was defensive. In practical terms, however, neither wanted the other side to establish control on the ground while the border remained unsettled.

## What was agreed in Siem Reap

At the Siem Reap meeting, Cambodian Foreign Minister Hor Namhong and his Thai counterpart, Tej Bunnag, sought to prevent the confrontation from escalating.

The two sides agreed to pursue a reduction and redeployment of troops around Preah Vihear, subject to approval and implementation by their governments and military authorities. They also agreed that the dispute should be addressed peacefully through bilateral channels, including the joint bodies responsible for surveying and demarcating the border.

The understanding was deliberately limited. It did not produce a final boundary, determine ownership of the disputed land or establish an immediate, comprehensive withdrawal timetable. Instead, it created a framework for easing the military pressure while technical and diplomatic negotiations continued.

That distinction was important. A complete withdrawal was difficult because both governments feared that pulling back first could be portrayed domestically as surrendering territory. Even decisions about where troops should redeploy depended on the very border interpretation that was in dispute.

## How UNESCO’s decision intensified tensions

UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee inscribed Preah Vihear on the World Heritage List on July 7, 2008. The listing recognized the temple’s architectural and cultural importance; it did not award sovereignty, redraw the border or overrule the 1962 International Court of Justice judgment.

Politically, however, the decision had consequences far beyond heritage conservation.

Cambodia presented the inscription as an international affirmation of a central part of its cultural patrimony. Prime Minister Hun Sen’s government celebrated it as a national achievement.

In Thailand, the issue became entangled with an intense domestic struggle between the government and its opponents. The administration of Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej had supported Cambodia’s bid through a joint communiqué. Thai nationalists and anti-government protesters accused the administration of compromising Thai territorial claims and helping Cambodia strengthen its position over the surrounding land.

Thailand’s Constitutional Court subsequently ruled that the government should have obtained parliamentary approval before endorsing the communiqué. Foreign Minister Noppadon Pattama resigned amid the controversy. The ruling and the political backlash weakened Bangkok’s ability to make concessions and transformed what had been a technical heritage issue into a test of patriotism and governmental legitimacy.

Cambodia, meanwhile, rejected suggestions that the listing threatened Thailand’s rights in unresolved border areas. Phnom Penh argued that the World Heritage property covered the temple under Cambodian sovereignty and that border demarcation could proceed separately.

The two sides were therefore talking about different legal and political questions. UNESCO was considering the protection of an ancient monument. Cambodia treated inscription as recognition of its stewardship of the temple. Thai critics feared that maps and management plans associated with the listing could prejudice negotiations over adjacent territory.

UNESCO itself had no authority to settle the border. But the prestige of the designation, the maps submitted with the nomination and the symbolism attached to the temple magnified public scrutiny of every military movement and diplomatic statement.

## A dispute shaped by law, maps and nationalism

The Preah Vihear confrontation illustrated the limits of the 1962 judgment. The ruling clearly settled ownership of the temple, but unresolved questions about nearby land remained vulnerable to political exploitation.

It also showed how domestic pressures constrained diplomacy. Cambodian leaders could not appear to tolerate what they described as a Thai incursion. Thai leaders, already under attack from nationalist opponents, could not easily withdraw from land they characterized as undemarcated.

The Siem Reap talks therefore represented crisis management rather than a settlement. By agreeing to reduce the military presence and return the issue to bilateral negotiations, the governments tried to separate immediate security concerns from the slower process of mapping the frontier.

But as long as the border remained incompletely demarcated, even a cultural designation intended to preserve a shared regional treasure could serve as a trigger for renewed confrontation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you report on the Cambodia-Thailand temple standoff and connect it to Hun Sen’s election victory, Thai domestic politics, and the International Court of Justice’s 1962 ruling?
counterfactuals.output:
## Cambodia–Thailand temple standoff

The confrontation centered on **Preah Vihear**, an 11th-century Khmer temple on the escarpment separating northern Cambodia from northeastern Thailand. Tensions surged in **July 2008**, after UNESCO placed the temple on its World Heritage List at Cambodia’s request.

Thailand had initially endorsed the application, which covered the temple itself rather than the surrounding disputed zone. But Thai nationalists argued that the endorsement weakened Thailand’s position over roughly **4.6 square kilometers of adjacent land**. After several Thai activists crossed into the area and were detained, both countries deployed troops near the temple. Exchanges of fire later occurred, and the dispute remained militarized for several years.

## Connection to Hun Sen’s election victory

The crisis unfolded immediately before Cambodia’s **July 27, 2008 parliamentary election**. Prime Minister **Hun Sen** and the Cambodian People’s Party presented the UNESCO listing and Cambodia’s firm response to Thailand as victories in defense of national heritage and sovereignty.

The CPP won **90 of 123 National Assembly seats**, consolidating Hun Sen’s rule. The temple dispute was not the sole reason—the CPP already benefited from incumbency, economic growth, patronage networks, and control of much of the media—but it gave Hun Sen a powerful nationalist issue. Opposition parties accused his government of exploiting the confrontation for electoral advantage. Conversely, Hun Sen could portray critics as insufficiently resolute toward Thailand.

## Thai domestic politics

On the Thai side, the dispute became entangled with the struggle between the government of Prime Minister **Samak Sundaravej**, aligned with ousted premier Thaksin Shinawatra, and the anti-Thaksin **People’s Alliance for Democracy** and its allies.

Thai Foreign Minister **Noppadon Pattama** had signed a communiqué supporting Cambodia’s UNESCO application. Nationalist groups charged that the government had surrendered Thai territory, while opponents linked the decision to Thaksin’s business and political relationship with Hun Sen. Thailand’s Constitutional Court ruled that the communiqué should have received parliamentary approval, prompting Noppadon’s resignation.

Thus, taking a hard line on Preah Vihear became politically useful in Bangkok. Civilian leaders faced strong pressure from protesters, courts, the opposition, and the military not to appear weak. This made compromise more difficult and turned a border-management problem into a symbol of the broader Thai political crisis.

## The International Court of Justice’s 1962 ruling

In **1962**, the International Court of Justice ruled that:

- **The Temple of Preah Vihear was situated in Cambodian territory**.
- Thailand had to withdraw military or police forces stationed at the temple or in its vicinity.
- Thailand had to return certain objects removed from the site.

The judgment relied heavily on Thailand’s long-standing acceptance of a French-era map placing the temple on the Cambodian side, even though Thailand argued that the watershed line specified in earlier treaties would place it differently.

Crucially, the 1962 judgment did **not comprehensively delimit the entire surrounding border**. Thailand accepted that the temple belonged to Cambodia but maintained that nearby land remained undemarcated. Cambodia argued that the judgment and its underlying map also supported Cambodian sovereignty over the temple’s immediate surroundings. This ambiguity helped fuel the 2008 standoff.

In **2013**, after renewed fighting, the ICJ interpreted its earlier judgment and held that Cambodia had sovereignty over the **whole promontory of Preah Vihear**, requiring Thai forces to withdraw from that area. It did not, however, settle every segment of the wider Cambodia–Thailand frontier.

## Bottom line

The standoff was simultaneously:

1. a genuine dispute over an incompletely demarcated colonial-era border;
2. a Cambodian nationalist success that strengthened Hun Sen during the 2008 election;
3. a weapon in Thailand’s anti-Thaksin political struggle; and
4. a consequence of the gap between the ICJ’s clear award of the temple to Cambodia and the less-complete settlement of the surrounding territory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**Thailand, Cambodia agree to troop pullback near disputed temple**

BANGKOK/PHNOM PENH — Thailand and Cambodia have agreed to pull back some soldiers stationed around the 11th-century Preah Vihear temple, easing a military standoff in a disputed stretch of their border, officials from both countries said.

The confrontation centers on about 1.8 square miles (4.6 square km) of land near the Hindu temple. The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962, but the surrounding boundary remains contested.

Tensions rose on July 15, when Cambodian authorities detained three Thai activists who crossed into the temple area to protest Cambodian control. They were later released, but troops from both countries moved into the vicinity, creating a standoff that lasted for weeks.

Cambodia says Thai soldiers crossed into Cambodian territory after the activists were detained and has described the deployment as an incursion. Thailand rejects that account, saying its troops remained on Thai soil and were sent to protect the border after Cambodia increased its military presence.

Under the pullback agreement, both sides will reduce troop numbers and reposition some forces away from the immediate temple area. Soldiers will remain elsewhere along the frontier while officials continue negotiations on the unresolved boundary.

Preah Vihear, perched on a cliff along the frontier, has long been a source of nationalist tension. The dispute intensified after UNESCO added the temple to its World Heritage list, a decision welcomed by Cambodia but opposed by some groups in Thailand who feared it could strengthen Phnom Penh’s territorial claims.

Officials portrayed the redeployment as a step toward reducing tensions, though it does not settle sovereignty over the disputed land. Further talks between military commanders and border negotiators are expected.
